title: About Vaultik
content:
Vaultik is building AI-first cybersecurity designed exclusively for financial services.

Banks and financial institutions face a unique threat landscape. Attackers don't just want data — they want money, access, and leverage. Off-the-shelf cybersecurity tools weren't built for the complexity of financial infrastructure, where a single breach can trigger regulatory action, customer flight, and systemic risk.

Vaultik changes the equation. Our AI-driven threat detection platform is purpose-built for the financial sector, understanding the specific patterns, protocols, and attack vectors that target banks, credit unions, wealth managers, and fintech companies. We detect threats that generic security tools miss because we understand how financial systems actually work.

Our platform monitors network traffic, transaction patterns, employee behavior, and third-party integrations in real time, using AI models trained specifically on financial services threat intelligence. When we detect something anomalous, we don't just alert — we provide context, impact assessment, and recommended response actions tailored to financial regulatory requirements.

Founded in 2024 by Tomas Herrera and Jade Washington, Vaultik is backed by AIVC and headquartered in Miami. Our founding team brings experience from Google DeepMind, JPMorgan Chase, and the NSA's Cybersecurity Directorate.

We're protecting the financial institutions that power the economy. Learn more at vaultik.com.

title: Vaultik — First Board Meeting Post-Investment
author: Sarah Chen
content:
Board Meeting — Vaultik
January 15, 2026 | 11:00 AM ET | Zoom

First formal board meeting since closing the seed round in October. Attendees: Tomás Herrera (CEO), Jade Washington (CTO), Sarah Chen (AIVC, Board Chair), James Morrison (AIVC).

## Company Status
- Team: 14 employees (up from 8 at close). 6 engineers, 3 data scientists, 2 product, 1 marketing, Tomás, Jade
- Customers: 4 (2 community banks, 1 credit union, 1 regional fintech lender)
- ARR: $420K
- Burn: $160K/mo
- Cash: $4.1M
- Runway: ~25 months at current burn

## Product Roadmap (Jade)
Jade walked through the product architecture and roadmap. I continue to be impressed with the technical depth here.

- Current platform: real-time network monitoring + AI anomaly detection. The AI models are trained on financial-services-specific threat intelligence data that Jade and team curated from public breach reports, NIST frameworks, and partnerships with 2 threat intelligence providers
- The secret sauce: their AI understands the difference between normal and abnormal behavior *in a banking context*. A large after-hours transaction might be normal for a trading desk but abnormal for a retail branch. Generic SIEM tools can't make that distinction without months of custom configuration
- Q1 2026 roadmap: transaction pattern monitoring (detecting fraudulent transaction patterns in real time), employee behavior analytics (flagging insider threats), and enhanced regulatory compliance reporting
- Q2-Q3 2026: API security module (protecting banking APIs from sophisticated attacks), third-party risk monitoring (assessing security of vendor integrations)
- Jade wants to hire 3 more engineers to hit this roadmap. 2 senior backend engineers and 1 ML engineer specializing in anomaly detection

## Go-to-Market (Tomás)
- Sales is 100% founder-led right now. Tomás is the only person selling
- Pipeline: 4 active conversations (2 community banks, 1 mid-size regional bank, 1 fintech)
- Sales cycle: 2-3 months for community banks, 4-6 months for larger institutions
- ACVs: $80-120K for community banks, potentially $200-400K for regional banks
- Tomás acknowledged that founder-led sales won't scale but said it's the right approach for now. He wants to hire a VP Sales or Head of Sales by Q3 2026, once they have 8-10 customers and a repeatable playbook

I pushed Tomás on the sales timeline. At 4 customers and $420K ARR, they need to accelerate customer acquisition. He agreed but said the financial services sales cycle is long and trust-based — banks don't buy security software from companies they don't know. He's investing in content marketing, conference speaking, and advisory board relationships to build credibility.

## Hiring Plan
- 3 engineers (Jade's request) — targeting Q1 hires
- 1 security analyst to help with customer onboarding and threat monitoring
- Head of Sales in Q3 2026
- Target: 22-24 employees by end of 2026

## Concerns Raised
- I flagged the concentration risk: 4 customers, all small institutions. We need to land a mid-size bank to prove the product works at scale
- James flagged competitive risk from Darktrace, which has announced a financial services division. Tomás said Darktrace is "a mile wide and an inch deep" in financial services — they're repurposing generic enterprise security for banks, not building from the ground up like Vaultik
- I asked about Jade's long-term commitment given her Google DeepMind background. Both she and Tomás said she's fully committed. Jade said she left DeepMind specifically because she wanted to build something that directly protects people's financial security. I'm taking that at face value for now but flagging for ongoing attention

## Action Items
1. Tomás: weekly pipeline updates to James via email
2. Jade: engineering hiring plan with JDs by end of January
3. Sarah: intro Tomás to 2-3 community bank CEOs in AIVC network
4. James: research competitive landscape (Darktrace, Abnormal Security, CrowdStrike) and share analysis by Feb 15
5. Next board meeting: April 2026

title: Monthly check-in with Tomás — progress, new customers, and a concern about Jade
author: James Morrison
content:
Monthly Check-in — Vaultik
April 17, 2026 | 2:00 PM ET | Zoom, 30 min

## Business Update
- ARR: $680K (up from $420K at Jan board meeting — strong progress)
- Customers: 6 (added 2 new community banks since January: Pacific Coast Community Bank and Heritage Savings Bank)
- Both new customers came through referrals from existing customers — great sign for product satisfaction
- Pipeline: 3 active deals, including one mid-size regional bank (Coastal National Bank, potential $250K ACV). Tomás has been working this for 3 months and feels optimistic
- Burn: $180K/mo (up from $160K due to new hires)
- Team: 17 employees. Hired 2 of the 3 engineers Jade wanted, plus the security analyst

## Product
- Transaction pattern monitoring shipped in March — all 6 customers are using it
- Employee behavior analytics in beta with 2 customers
- Jade and Victor Nkomo (Head of Engineering) are working well together. Victor is managing the day-to-day engineering while Jade focuses on AI/ML architecture
- Tomás showed me a demo of the new regulatory compliance reporting module — generates automated reports aligned with OCC and FDIC examination requirements. This is a killer feature for community banks that hate manual compliance work

## The Jade Situation
Tomás brought something up near the end of the call, and he was clearly uncomfortable about it.

Jade received an offer from Google DeepMind. Not just any offer — a senior research scientist position on their applied AI team, working on financial systems. The offer came through a former colleague who's now a director there.

Tomás said Jade told him about it a few days ago. She hasn't accepted and said she wants to stay at Vaultik, but Tomás is worried. The comp gap is significant — DeepMind is reportedly offering $550-600K total comp (base + bonus + RSUs). Jade's current Vaultik comp is $200K base + equity, which is obviously a different equation.

Tomás asked if AIVC could help think through retention options. He mentioned:
- Equity refresh (additional grant to increase Jade's ownership stake)
- Retention bonus
- Possibly a co-founder title (Jade joined as employee #1 but wasn't technically a co-founder)

I told Tomás this is exactly the kind of thing we should involve Sarah in — she's dealt with CTO retention situations before. Suggested he email Sarah directly.

My read: this is a serious risk. Jade IS the technical differentiation at Vaultik. Without her, the AI models, the financial-services-specific threat intelligence, the entire technical vision — it all gets much harder. Victor is good but he's an execution-oriented engineering manager, not a technical visionary.

Flagging this to Sarah immediately after this call.

## Other Notes
- Tomás is still doing all the selling himself. He's good at it but it's eating his time. He said the Coastal National Bank deal has required 6 in-person meetings in the past 2 months
- He wants to start thinking about Series A positioning. I suggested Q4 2026 / Q1 2027 if they can get to $1.5M+ ARR and 10+ customers
- He asked about competitive intelligence on Abnormal Security's recent fundraise ($250M Series C). I said I'd loop back with research

ACTION: Flag Jade retention risk to Sarah ASAP

title: Confidential — Call with Jade Washington re: retention
author: Sarah Chen
content:
CONFIDENTIAL — Retention Discussion
Call with Jade Washington — May 6, 2026
45 min | Zoom | Sarah Chen

Context: After James flagged the DeepMind offer in his April check-in with Tomás, I reached out to Jade directly to have an honest conversation about where her head is at.

## The DeepMind Offer
- Jade confirmed: Google DeepMind offered her a Senior Research Scientist position, L6 equivalent. Applied AI team focused on financial systems (fraud detection, risk modeling)
- Total comp: ~$580K/year (base $280K + bonus + RSUs). This is roughly 2.5x her current Vaultik cash comp
- The role would be research-oriented with publication opportunities. For someone who came from an academic ML background, this is appealing
- The former colleague who recruited her (Dr. Kira Patel, now a Director at DeepMind) is someone Jade deeply respects

## Jade's Perspective
- She was candid with me, which I appreciate. She said she has NOT accepted and genuinely does not want to leave Vaultik
- Her reasons for wanting to stay: she believes in the mission, she loves the team (especially Victor and two junior engineers she's mentoring), and she wants to build something from the ground up rather than be a cog at Google
- Her concerns: comp gap is real and hard to ignore. She's 32, has student loans from her PhD, and her partner is a public school teacher. The financial pressure is not trivial
- She also mentioned feeling like she needs more recognition for her role — she was the first employee, built all the core technology, but doesn't have a co-founder title. She said this is not about ego but about the signal it sends to the team and to the market

## What I Proposed
I told Jade that AIVC wants to help find a solution that works for everyone. I outlined several options that I'd discussed with David in advance:

1. Equity refresh: an additional 1.5-2% grant vesting over 4 years, on top of her existing equity. This would make Jade one of the largest equity holders outside of Tomás
2. Cash retention bonus: $75-100K paid over 2 years, contingent on continued employment
3. Co-founder title: I suggested this to Tomás and he was open to it. Jade would officially become co-founder and CTO
4. Conference and research budget: $20K/year for Jade to attend and speak at ML/security conferences, maintain her academic profile

Jade seemed genuinely moved by the conversation. She said no one from the investor side had ever taken the time to understand her perspective this directly.

She asked for 2 weeks to discuss with her partner and think it through. I told her to take whatever time she needs and that the offer is real, not a negotiating tactic.

## My Assessment
- I think we can retain Jade, but it's not a slam dunk. The comp gap is significant even with the retention package
- The co-founder title matters more than I initially thought. It's about belonging and recognition
- If we lose Jade, Vaultik's valuation and technical trajectory take a serious hit. She's not easily replaceable — the combination of DeepMind-caliber ML skills and financial services domain expertise is extremely rare
- I've told Tomás to prepare contingency plans (promoting Victor, identifying external CTO candidates) just in case, but emphasized that retention is the primary strategy
- Timeline: Jade said she'd give us an answer by May 20. DeepMind wants a response by end of May

NOTE: This is a confidential document. Do not share details outside of Sarah, David, and James.

title: Cybersecurity Startups Target Banks as Financial Sector AI Threats Grow
author: William Turton
content:
Cybersecurity Startups Target Banks as Financial Sector AI Threats Grow
By William Turton | Bloomberg | March 12, 2026

As artificial intelligence makes cyberattacks more sophisticated, a new wave of startups is building security tools designed specifically for the financial sector — betting that banks need more than generic enterprise security to protect themselves.

The threat landscape for financial institutions has shifted dramatically in the past two years. AI-powered phishing attacks now mimic the writing style of specific executives. Deepfake voice technology has been used in at least three confirmed cases to impersonate bank officers and authorize fraudulent wire transfers. And automated vulnerability scanning tools have made it easier for attackers to find weaknesses in the complex web of APIs and integrations that modern banks depend on.

"The financial sector is facing threats that didn't exist three years ago," said Rob Lee, CEO of Dragos and a former NSA analyst. "Generic cybersecurity tools are built to protect generic enterprises. Banks are not generic enterprises."

Several startups are racing to fill this gap. Vaultik, a Miami-based startup founded in 2024, has built an AI-driven threat detection platform designed exclusively for banks and financial institutions. CEO Tomás Herrera, a former JPMorgan Chase cybersecurity executive, said the company's AI models are trained specifically on financial services threat intelligence, allowing them to detect attack patterns that generic security tools would miss.

"When we see anomalous behavior in a banking environment, we understand the context," Herrera said. "A large wire transfer at 2 AM means something different at a global trading desk than at a community bank branch. Our AI knows the difference."

Vaultik has signed six community banks and regional financial institutions, and Herrera said the company is in advanced discussions with several larger banks. The company raised a $4.5 million seed round from AIVC in October 2025.

The opportunity is attracting larger players as well. Darktrace, the UK-based cybersecurity company with a market cap of roughly $4 billion, recently announced a dedicated Financial Services Division, assigning more than 50 engineers to build bank-specific detection models. Abnormal Security, which specializes in AI-powered email security, raised $250 million in a Series C in April and said financial services is its fastest-growing vertical.

CrowdStrike, the market leader in endpoint security, has also expanded its financial services practice, launching a dedicated banking threat intelligence feed in January.

But startups like Vaultik argue that financial-services-specific incumbents and dedicated newcomers have an advantage over general-purpose security platforms that bolt on financial features.

"You can't just add a 'banking mode' to a generic SIEM and call it financial services security," said Jade Washington, CTO of Vaultik and a former Google DeepMind researcher. "The threat models are fundamentally different. The regulatory requirements are different. The attack surfaces are different. You have to build from the ground up."

Bank CISOs appear to agree, at least in principle. A survey by Deloitte found that 67% of financial institution security leaders plan to adopt at least one AI-powered security tool in 2026, and 45% expressed a preference for solutions designed specifically for financial services.

The market is still early, and it remains to be seen whether specialized financial security startups can compete with the massive sales and support organizations of incumbents like CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks. But as AI-powered threats continue to evolve, the argument for financial-sector-specific security is only getting stronger.

title: Abnormal Security Raises $250M Series C for AI Email Security
author: Carly Page
content:
Abnormal Security Raises $250M Series C for AI Email Security
By Carly Page | TechCrunch | April 2, 2026

Abnormal Security, the San Francisco-based startup that uses AI to detect and prevent email-based attacks, has raised $250 million in a Series C funding round, valuing the company at $5.1 billion.

The round was led by Wellington Management and Greenoaks Capital, with participation from existing investors CrowdStrike Falcon Fund, Greylock Partners, and Menlo Ventures.

CEO Evan Reiser said the funding will be used to expand Abnormal's platform beyond email into adjacent communication channels (Slack, Teams, SMS), deepen its financial services vertical, and accelerate international expansion.

"Email is the number one attack vector, and it's getting worse with AI-generated phishing," Reiser told TechCrunch. "But email is just the starting point. We're building the behavioral AI platform that protects every communication channel in the enterprise."

Abnormal's technology uses behavioral AI to learn the normal communication patterns of every employee in an organization, then detects anomalies that indicate phishing, business email compromise, or social engineering attacks. The company says it has blocked over 500 million attacks across its 2,300+ customers.

Financial services is Abnormal's fastest-growing vertical, accounting for approximately 25% of new customer acquisitions. The company said banks and financial institutions face particularly sophisticated email attacks, including AI-generated communications that mimic the writing style of executives and board members.

The fundraise comes amid a broader wave of investment in AI-powered cybersecurity. Darktrace recently announced a dedicated financial services division, and smaller players like Vaultik and Halcyon are building specialized security tools for specific industries.

Abnormal has approximately 600 employees and reported that its ARR exceeded $200 million in Q1 2026. The company said it grew revenue over 100% year-over-year.

title: Darktrace Reports Accelerating Enterprise Revenue, Announces Financial Services Division
author: Hannah Murphy
content:
Darktrace Reports Accelerating Enterprise Revenue, Announces Financial Services Division
By Hannah Murphy | Financial Times | February 18, 2026

Darktrace, the UK-based cybersecurity group, reported accelerating enterprise revenue growth in its latest quarterly results and announced the creation of a dedicated Financial Services Division aimed at capturing a larger share of the banking and insurance security market.

The company said enterprise revenue grew 28% year-over-year in the quarter ending December 2025, up from 22% growth in the prior quarter. Total revenue for the period was $165 million, with the company reporting 9,200 customers globally.

CEO Poppy Gustafsson said the financial services push reflects growing demand from banks for AI-powered security tools that understand the specific threats facing the industry.

"Financial institutions are under siege from increasingly sophisticated adversaries, and they recognise that traditional security approaches are insufficient," Gustafsson said during an earnings call. "We're dedicating significant engineering and go-to-market resources to serve this critical market."

The Financial Services Division will include more than 50 engineers building bank-specific threat detection models, as well as a dedicated sales team targeting large banks and insurance companies. Darktrace said it already serves approximately 400 financial institutions, including several global systemically important banks.

The announcement positions Darktrace more directly against specialist financial security providers, as well as larger competitors like CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks. Several startups, including Miami-based Vaultik, have argued that purpose-built financial security tools are more effective than general-purpose platforms adapted for banking.

Analysts at Jefferies said the financial services push could add significant revenue if executed well. "Financial services is a high-value vertical with complex security needs and relatively low price sensitivity," they wrote in a note. "But execution risk is real — Darktrace needs to demonstrate that it can deliver financial-services-specific capabilities, not just relabel its existing product."

Darktrace shares rose 6% following the earnings report. The company's market capitalisation is approximately $4.2 billion.

title: Vaultik — Q1 2026 Investor Update
author: Tomás Herrera
content:
From: Tomás Herrera <tomas@vaultik.com>
To: investors@vaultik.com
Date: April 9, 2026
Subject: Vaultik — Q1 2026 Investor Update

Dear Investors,

I'm excited to share our Q1 2026 update. Six months after closing our seed round, Vaultik is building momentum.

Key Metrics (Q1 2026)
- ARR: $680K (up from $420K at time of investment)
- Customers: 6 (up from 4)
- Monthly burn: $180K
- Cash: $3.5M
- Runway: ~19 months
- Headcount: 17

Highlights

We signed two new customers in Q1: Pacific Coast Community Bank and Heritage Savings Bank. Both came through referrals from our existing customers, which tells me two things: the product is working and our customers are willing to vouch for us. For a security product, that kind of trust-based referral is gold.

Our ARR grew 62% from investment close to end of Q1. I know we're starting from a small base, but the trajectory is encouraging.

Product milestones:
- Shipped transaction pattern monitoring (real-time detection of anomalous financial transactions) in March. All 6 customers deployed it within 2 weeks of release
- Employee behavior analytics is in beta with 2 customers. Early results are strong — one bank identified a suspicious access pattern from a contractor that turned out to be a credential-sharing issue
- Regulatory compliance reporting module is in development (targeting Q2 release). This auto-generates reports aligned with OCC and FDIC examination requirements. Every community bank CTO I've talked to says this alone would justify the purchase

Team

We're at 17 people and growing. Key hires in Q1:
- 2 senior backend engineers (one from Cloudflare, one from CrowdStrike)
- 1 security analyst for customer onboarding and threat monitoring

Still looking for: 1 ML engineer (specializing in anomaly detection), 2 more backend engineers, and eventually a Head of Sales.

Jade Washington and Victor Nkomo continue to be the engine of our technical team. Jade is architecting the AI models while Victor manages the engineering execution. They work well together.

Concerns

I want to be transparent about the challenges:

1. Sales is still founder-led. I'm closing every deal personally. This works at our current scale but will not work at 15-20 customers. I'm planning to hire a Head of Sales in Q3, but need to develop a repeatable playbook first.

2. Competition is intensifying. Darktrace announced a dedicated Financial Services Division in February. Abnormal Security raised $250M and is pushing into financial services. We're differentiated by our ground-up financial services architecture, but we need to move fast while our technical advantage holds.

3. We need to land a larger customer. Our 6 customers are community banks and small institutions. To prove the product scales, we need to win a mid-size regional bank. I have one in late-stage pipeline (Coastal National Bank, $250K ACV potential) but the sales cycle is long.

4. Team key-person risk. We're a small team and our technical capability is concentrated. I'm focused on building depth across the engineering team to reduce single points of failure.

Looking Ahead (Q2 2026)
- Close Coastal National Bank
- Ship compliance reporting module
- Hire 3 engineers
- Begin developing sales playbook for eventual Head of Sales hire
- Target: $0.8M-$1.0M ARR by end of Q2

Thank you for your partnership. I'm grateful for AIVC's hands-on support — Sarah and James have been valuable thought partners on both strategy and execution.

Tomás Herrera
CEO, Vaultik
